chunks: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Taleqani narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Hamadani narrated to us, from Ali ibn Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhdhal, from his father, from Abu Al-Hasan Ali ibn Musa (peace be upon him)

He said: Whoever fasts the first day of Rajab with desire for the reward of Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, Paradise becomes obligatory for him. And whoever fasts a day in its middle, intercession is accepted for him equal to the number of people in the tribes of Rabi'ah and Mudar. And whoever fasts a day in its end, Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, makes him one of the kings of Paradise, and accepts his intercession for his father, mother, son, daughter, brother, sister, paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, maternal aunt, acquaintances, and neighbors, even if some of them deserve the Fire.

key_terms.رَبِيعَةَ وَمُضَرَ: Rabi'ah and Mudar (major Arab tribes, used to denote large numbers)
key_terms.رَجَب: Rajab (the seventh month of the Islamic lunar calendar)
key_terms.شَفَّعَهُ: He was interceded for / His intercession was accepted
key_terms.مُسْتَوْجِبٌ لِلنَّارِ: Deserving of the Fire (one who merits hellfire)
key_terms.مُلُوكِ الْجَنَّةِ: Kings of Paradise (a high rank in the afterlife)

ai.seo_question: What are the rewards of fasting on the first, middle, and last days of Rajab according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This tradition from Imam al-Rida (s) in *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida* emphasizes the unique in its specific attribution of distinct eschatological rewards to the first, middle, and last days of Rajab, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the sanctity of this month as a precursor to Ramadan. The mention of intercession (*shafa'ah*) for family and even those deserving of Hellfire highlights the concept of *shafa'ah al-kubra* and the expansive mercy of the Ahl al-Bayt, while the promise of becoming a 'king in Paradise' underscores the high spiritual status attained through such devotions.
